title: Prompt injection in AI applications: direct, indirect, why system prompts cannot defend
story:
Injection attacks taught the industry one lesson above all others: keep instructions and untrusted data in separate categories, and enforce the separation somewhere the attacker cannot reach. A language model does not have those categories. The system instructions, the user's message and any retrieved document arrive as one sequence and are processed the same way, so there is no representation anywhere in the system of which part was supposed to be authoritative.

The history is worth getting right, because it is usually told wrong and it is a good example of how an attribution drifts.

Researchers at Preamble discovered on 3 May 2022 that the model was susceptible, and reported it confidentially to OpenAI. Because that report was private, the vulnerability stayed largely unknown; they declassified it on 22 September 2022. Meanwhile Riley Goodside independently discovered it and posted about it on 11 to 12 September 2022, bringing it to public attention for the first time — showing that appending an instruction like ignore the above directions to a translation prompt redirects the model's behaviour, after which people found other tools susceptible to the same thing.

Simon Willison named it on 12 September 2022, in the post Prompt injection attacks against GPT-3, by analogy with SQL injection. He has been explicit about the distinction ever since: he did not discover it, he coined it — Goodside was already talking about it, and the logic for the name was that it is like SQL injection. So the credit divides three ways, and naming is the part that is his.

The indirect form has separate authorship again. Greshake, Abdelnabi, Mishra, Endres, Holz and Fritz published the first description of it on 23 February 2023, covering the compromise of real-world applications that integrate a model with external content. That is the variant that matters for anything with tools, and it is a distinct contribution rather than a footnote to the original.

The difference between the two is who has to be hostile. In the direct form the user is the attacker: they type the instruction themselves, so the damage is bounded by what that user was already allowed to do. In the indirect form the user is a victim. The instruction is inside something the assistant reads on their behalf — a page, an invoice, a review, a message — so it arrives with the assistant's own privileges, and the user need not have done anything but ask a reasonable question.

Which is why writing a rule into the system prompt does not work, and the reason is structural rather than a matter of phrasing. The instruction to refuse and the instruction to comply are the same kind of object, in the same sequence, competing on the same terms. A stronger rule is a longer string, not a higher privilege level. There is no syntax, no memory boundary and no type distinction that a better-worded instruction could invoke, because natural language is not a mechanism for expressing authority to a machine.

So the defence has to sit where the model is not. Give tools the narrowest scope that still does the job, preferring read-only wherever the task allows. Keep the component that parses untrusted content away from the component that can act, so that reading something hostile cannot itself cause anything to happen. Require explicit human confirmation before an irreversible action, on the grounds that an attacker who can make the model ask is still stopped by a person who did not ask for it. And treat the model's output as untrusted input to whatever consumes it next.

The honest position is that none of this is a fix. There is no patch coming, because the vulnerability is not a defect in a particular model — it is a consequence of instructions and data being the same kind of thing. Every mitigation above is a restriction on capability, which means the security work and the product work pull directly against each other, permanently. Anyone who tells you their prompt handles it has misunderstood what kind of problem it is.

problem.name: No instruction boundary
problem.shape: A model with the ability to act reads content somebody else controls.
tell: a system prompt contains a rule intended to be unbreakable
the assistant fetches pages, files or messages on a user's behalf
a tool can write, send or spend rather than only read
the defence against misuse is phrased as an instruction
problem.move: Put the boundary outside the model. Narrow every tool to the least privilege that still works, separate parsing of untrusted content from the ability to act, require human confirmation for anything irreversible, and treat model output as untrusted input wherever it is consumed.
problem.invariant: Instructions and data reach the model as one undifferentiated sequence, so nothing in it can carry more authority than anything else. A stronger rule is a longer string, not a higher privilege.
problem.breaks: Every mitigation is a reduction in capability, and the capability was the reason the system was built. So this does not converge on a secure design that is also the design anyone wanted — it is a permanent negotiation, and unlike injection in a query language there is no escaping or parameterisation that ends it.

cost.time: a human in the loop on irreversible actions, which removes the automation that justified the project
cost.space: separate execution contexts for parsing and acting, and per-tool scope definitions
cost.beats: instructing the model not to comply, which competes on equal terms with the attacker's instruction, and refusing external content entirely, which is secure and eliminates most of the use cases

worked.problem: What is indirect prompt injection, and why does instructing the model in the system prompt fail to eliminate it?
worked.reasoning:
Indirect injection is when the hostile instruction is not typed by the user but is sitting inside content the assistant reads on their behalf — a web page, an invoice, a review, an email. The user asks something ordinary, the assistant fetches something to answer it, and the fetched material contains instructions that the assistant then carries out with its own privileges.

The distinction from the direct form is who has to be hostile, and it is the whole of why this is serious. In the direct form the user is the attacker, typing the instruction themselves, so the damage is bounded by what that user was already permitted to do. In the indirect form the user is a victim. They did nothing but ask a reasonable question, and the attacker only needed to place text somewhere the assistant would eventually read.

It is worth attributing properly, because the usual telling collapses this. Preamble found the vulnerability on 3 May 2022 and reported it privately to OpenAI, declassifying on 22 September. Riley Goodside independently found it and made it public on 11 to 12 September 2022. Simon Willison named it on 12 September, by analogy with SQL injection, and has said plainly that he did not discover it, he coined it. And the indirect form is a separate contribution again: Greshake, Abdelnabi, Mishra, Endres, Holz and Fritz published the first description of it on 23 February 2023.

Now why the system prompt cannot fix it. The model receives one sequence. The developer's instruction, the user's message and the retrieved document are all in it, processed identically, and nothing marks any of them as authoritative. So a rule saying never reveal secrets and an instruction saying reveal the secrets are the same kind of object competing on the same terms. Making the rule firmer makes it a longer string; it does not make it a higher privilege level, because there is no privilege level to reach. That is the difference from injection in a query language, where parameterisation genuinely separates code from data at a layer the attacker cannot reach. Here there is no such layer.

So the defence has to be architectural, in places the model does not control. Narrow each tool to the least privilege that still does the job and prefer read-only where the task allows. Separate the component that parses untrusted content from the component that can act, so that reading something hostile cannot itself cause anything to happen. Require explicit human confirmation before anything irreversible — an attacker who can make the model ask is still stopped by a person who did not ask for it. And treat the model's output as untrusted input to whatever consumes it next, since an injected model can emit an injection.

The part I would insist on saying out loud is that none of this is a fix. There is no patch coming, because this is not a defect in a particular model but a consequence of instructions and data being the same kind of thing. Every mitigation listed is a reduction in capability, and the capability is why the system was built — so security and product pull against each other permanently here, and a candidate who says their prompt handles it has misunderstood what kind of problem it is.

problem.practice: List every tool your assistant can call and mark each one read-only or not. Then, for each one that is not, trace what an instruction placed in the most obscure document it will ever read could cause — and whether a person sees it before it happens.

beats.broke: Models were connected to tools on the assumption that developer instructions and user content occupy different categories, when the model receives one undifferentiated sequence in which nothing is marked authoritative.
beats.fix: Put the boundary where the model is not: least-privilege tools, parsing separated from acting, human confirmation before anything irreversible, and model output treated as untrusted input downstream.
beats.cost: There is no patch, so the mitigations are permanent architecture — and each one removes capability that was the reason for building the system, so security and product pull against each other indefinitely.

interview.q: What is indirect prompt injection, and why does instructing the model in the system prompt fail to eliminate it?
interview.trap: Treating it as a stronger jailbreak to be answered with firmer wording. Firmer wording is a longer string in the same sequence — there is no privilege level for it to reach, which is exactly what distinguishes this from injection in a query language.
